title: Rattle his bones
html_source:
An allusion to the poem A Pauper’s Drive by Thomas Noel, about a dead pauper being roughly conveyed to the cemetery in a cheap hearse. The driver shouts: “Rattle his bones, over the stones, he’s only a pauper, whom nobody owns.”
https://www.bartleby.com/71/1414.html

The “nobody owns” phrase comes a few lines later.

Much earlier in the chapter, the men complain about the shoddy carriage (not a “commodious yoke”) in which they are riding.

Just before this, Bloom thinks both lines of this poem. The first time, they seem to be a reference to Paddy Dignam, the dead man in whose cortege Bloom is rolling “over the stones.” The repetition here seems to be more referential to Bloom’s father – his next thoughts explicitly about his father’s suicide. There is also the intervening thought about the death of Bloom’s son Rudy after seeing a child’s casket hurrying on its way to the funeral.

As often happens with Joyce, these thoughts can coexist, informing each other.

Throughout this chapter, Joyce evokes Odysseus' time in Hades by having Bloom encounter many of the dead.
